title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: Why does AI ownership have no default owner?
options: Because the technology is too new for governance conventions to have formed
Because it is not a function — it lands inside every function at once, so each executive can see a piece that is genuinely theirs
Because most executive teams lack the technical understanding to assign it
Because regulators have not specified where accountability should sit
questions.explanation: Which is also why confidence in that room tells you nothing. Everyone is confident because everyone is looking at a real piece of it.

questions.prompt: What does the module predict about how the question gets settled?
options: Through a formal governance review once the risks become material
By precedent rather than principle — whoever moves first, builds the thing that works, or is in the room when the CEO asks
By the CEO, using a framework supplied by the Chief Digital Officer
By regulators, once employment AI obligations take effect
questions.explanation: And the consequence is the one that matters: a scope question decided by default is decided against the function that wasn't present.

options: That AI agents will replace a substantial proportion of the workforce
That HR should manage the technology because it affects employees

That if agents have owners, budgets, access rights, performance standards, onboarding and offboarding, that is workforce management — and those are disciplines your function already has and no other executive does
That agents should be counted in headcount reporting for budget purposes
questions.explanation: The strength is in the list rather than the metaphor. Each item is a discipline with an existing owner, and no other executive has an equivalent.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest objection to that argument? `[V]`
options: That agent technology is changing too quickly for stable ownership

That agents are software, the transferable disciplines are infrastructure ones that other functions already do well, and the CPO who wins may inherit operational work they are the wrong function to carry
That other executives would resist the claim on principle
That employment law does not recognize software as labour
questions.explanation: And the sharper version is that winning could be the worst outcome, acquiring operating-system overhead exactly when Module 2 argued your attention should move out of it.

questions.prompt: Why does "HR should own AI governance" lose as a claim?
options: Because governance is legally the General Counsel's responsibility
Because it is a claim about authority in a room where every other claimant has one too, so it reduces to who the CEO likes best
Because HR lacks the technical credibility to make it
Because governance is a subset of a larger ownership question
questions.explanation: It also carries an implication everyone hears (that the excluded function should now lead) without supplying a reason.

questions.prompt: What does the module offer as the claim that actually survives?
options: Joint ownership shared between the CPO and the CIO
A named decision right — no agent deployed into a process affecting a person's work, pay, evaluation or access without your sign-off
A seat on the AI steering committee with veto authority
Ownership of the agent registry and its associated budget
questions.explanation: Narrower, harder to refuse, doesn't require anyone else to lose something they wanted, and doesn't put you on call at 3am. D is close to the thing the module warns against acquiring.

questions.prompt: A significant AI decision has already been made without the CPO. What does the module recommend?
options: Relitigating the selection, since it was made without the affected function
Accepting the decision and focusing on adoption support
Claiming the consequences — what happens to the people whose work changes, the policy for what it may touch, the measurement, and who is accountable when it harms a named individual
Escalating to the CEO to establish precedent for future decisions
questions.explanation: Relitigating loses, costs the relationship, and the decision is sunk. The consequences are the more durable half of the scope, and nobody else wants them.

questions.prompt: What does the module require of a decline?
options: That it be escalated to the CEO for confirmation
That it be temporary and revisited within a defined period
That it be defensible in writing — what you are not claiming, what you require anyway, and what you are doing instead with the attention
That another executive formally accept the responsibility being declined
questions.explanation: Without those three parts, a decline is simply absence, which is the 52% outcome with extra steps rather than a decision.
